stories.headline: FED RATE-HIKE ODDS JUMP TOWARD 85% FOR DEC. 9 AFTER HAWKISH DISSENTS, 10-YEAR TOPS 4.95%
stories.body: CME FedWatch pricing swung sharply this week to show roughly an 85% probability the Fed raises rates at its Dec. 9 meeting, after two FOMC members dissented in favor of a hike at the Oct. 28 meeting where the committee held its target range at 3.75%-4%. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed 6 bps to 4.95% as traders repriced away from rate cuts, citing inflation risk from elevated energy prices.
stories.explain: Fed funds futures embed the market's probability-weighted expectation of the policy rate, and FedWatch simply backs that probability out of the futures price; when two sitting governors dissent toward tightening, traders infer the committee's reaction function has shifted hawkish, and that repriced the whole curve within a day. A rising 10-year yield alongside rising hike odds is mechanically intuitive: investors demand more compensation to hold duration when the expected path of short rates is higher, and bond prices move inversely to yields.

stories.headline: WALL STREET STAYS RANGEBOUND AS MIDTERM POLLS CLOSE, PREDICTION MARKETS PRICE 75%+ ODDS OF A DEMOCRATIC SWEEP
stories.body: Prediction markets priced better than 75% odds of a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress as polls closed Tuesday evening, a result traders are watching for its implications for fiscal policy, trade tariffs, and future Fed-board appointments. The S&P 500 held a tight band for most of the session, finishing up 0.35% at 7,569 as investors largely kept positioning steady ahead of results.
stories.explain: Elections move markets less through the vote itself than through the policy paths they unlock — a shift in congressional control changes the odds of extending or reversing tariff authority, spending bills, and the pace of future Fed appointments, and that shows up first in options-implied volatility rather than in the cash index before results are known. That's why today's S&P move stayed muted despite the stakes: implied vol tends to spike into a binary event and collapse once the uncertainty resolves, a classic 'vol crush' pattern.

stories.headline: CHIP RALLY LIFTS NASDAQ 100 AS AMD, ARISTA TOP FORECASTS; APPLE'S MARGIN WARNING STILL WEIGHS ON THE TAPE
stories.body: AMD and Arista Networks both topped Wall Street's sales estimates in results reported after Tuesday's close, sending both stocks higher in extended trading and capping a session in which chip names helped push the Nasdaq 100 up 0.66% to 28,180. The gains came one session after Apple's Nov. 2 report, in which management guided gross margin toward the high-40% range and the stock sold off, a drag that's kept pressure on the broader tape since.
stories.explain: Guidance, not trailing results, usually drives the stock reaction because the share price already embeds consensus expectations for the quarter just reported — what moves shares is whether forward numbers beat or miss the model, not the backward-looking print. AMD's and Arista's forecasts beating already-elevated expectations signal continued capex strength in AI infrastructure, while Apple's margin guide below its historical run rate signaled rising component and tariff-related costs eating into forward profitability, which is why the two earnings reactions pulled the index in opposite directions within the same week.

stories.headline: GOLD HOLDS NEAR $3,940 AS DOLLAR AND YIELDS FIRM INTO ELECTION NIGHT
stories.body: Spot gold ticked up 0.19% to roughly $3,940 an ounce even as the dollar index rose 0.09% to 101.87 and the 10-year yield climbed to 4.95% — a combination that would typically pressure gold, given it pays no yield. WTI crude slipped 0.33% to about $97 a barrel, holding near multi-month highs on an elevated geopolitical risk premium.
stories.explain: Gold normally trades inversely to real yields and the dollar because higher rates raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset, so today's simultaneous gains in gold, yields, and the dollar point to a separate bid — likely safe-haven positioning around election-night uncertainty and continued central-bank buying — temporarily overriding the usual relationship. Crude's pullback near $97 still keeps it a live input into next week's CPI print, since energy costs flow directly into both headline inflation and the inflation expectations the Fed is now citing as a reason to weigh another hike.

stories.headline: S&P 500, NASDAQ 100 EKE OUT GAINS AS TRADERS LOOK PAST ELECTION NOISE TO THIS WEEK'S JOBS DATA
stories.body: The S&P 500 added 0.35% to 7,569 and the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.66% to 28,180 Tuesday, with chip-sector strength offsetting Apple-related weakness, while the 10-year yield's climb to 4.95% capped gains in rate-sensitive sectors. Attention now turns to Thursday's jobs report and next week's CPI release, the last major data points before the Fed's Dec. 9 decision.
stories.explain: With rate-hike odds now the dominant market narrative, upcoming data carries outsized weight because each print can swing the Fed-funds-futures-implied probability by double digits in a single session — a hot CPI would likely push hike odds further above 85%, while a soft print could unwind much of today's yield move. That data dependency is exactly why volatility tends to cluster around scheduled releases rather than trading randomly through the month.

watchlist: Nonfarm payrolls Thursday, Nov. 5, 8:30 AM ET — first clean jobs read since shutdown-delayed data
CPI release Tuesday, Nov. 10 — last major inflation print before the Dec. 9 FOMC decision
FOMC meeting Dec. 9 — CME FedWatch pricing roughly 85% odds of a quarter-point hike
Midterm election results finalize control of Congress, with implications for fiscal and trade policy

deepDive.title: How Fed Funds Futures Turn a Vote Into a Probability
content: Today's brief leans on one number that would have sounded strange a few weeks ago: an 85% probability the Fed hikes rates on Dec. 9, derived from the CME FedWatch tool, with the 10-year yield already up 6 bps to 4.95% in response. For a finance student, the interesting part isn't that the Fed might raise rates — it's that a committee vote and two dissents got translated, within hours, into a single precise percentage that moved the entire Treasury curve. Understanding how that number is built explains why markets react so fast to Fed-adjacent news, and why today's yield move is not an overreaction but a mechanical repricing.

FedWatch doesn't survey anyone; it extracts probability from 30-day Fed funds futures prices. Each contract's price equals 100 minus the average effective fed funds rate the market expects for that delivery month, so a contract priced at 95.80 implies an expected average rate of 4.20%. Because the Fed only moves in known increments — typically 25 bps — and only at scheduled meetings, the tool can solve a simple weighted-average equation: if the current rate is 4.00% and the futures-implied rate for the December contract is 4.21%, the market must be pricing roughly an 84% chance of a 25 bp hike and a 16% chance of no move, since 0.84 × 4.25% + 0.16 × 4.00% ≈ 4.21%. That arithmetic, not a poll or a model, is where today's 85% figure comes from.

What most people miss is how sensitive that number is to the composition of a vote, not just its outcome. The Fed held rates steady on Oct. 28, but Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a hike — a hawkish dissent, where officials wanted tighter policy than the majority delivered. Markets treat dissents as information about the committee's future reaction function: a 10-2 vote with hawkish dissenters signals the center of gravity on the FOMC has shifted, even though the policy rate itself didn't change that day. A similar dynamic played out in 2022, when hawkish commentary from regional Fed presidents repeatedly moved futures-implied hike odds well before any actual rate decision, underscoring that FedWatch prices expectations about the committee, not just its last action.

That mechanism is exactly why Thursday's jobs report and next week's CPI print matter so much more than an ordinary data release. Each print gets fed back into the same futures pricing: a hot CPI number raises the market's implied probability that the Fed needs to hike to contain inflation, which should push the December-contract price down and the implied rate up, mechanically dragging the 10-year yield higher again. A soft print does the reverse. Because the probability is a continuous, market-derived number rather than a fixed forecast, it will keep moving — sometimes by ten points in a single session — right up until the Dec. 9 decision itself removes the uncertainty it was pricing.
